hook: GenAI architecture isn't a technology problem — it's a judgment problem. **This reel hands you the working architect's kit: selection matrices, NFR checklists, cost models, and the gates between POC and production.**

scenes.title: Use-case selection & ROI: kill weak use-cases early
scenes.sub: The 2x2 that decides what gets built — before anyone writes a prompt
scenes.narration: Most GenAI programs drown in use-cases — every department has ten. The architect's first job is selection, and it has two axes. VALUE: revenue gained, cost removed, risk reduced, experience improved — insist on a measurable baseline, because 'faster' without a number is a vibe; and FEASIBILITY: is the output verifiable, is the tolerance for error high, is the data available, is a human in the loop acceptable — GA-01's truth: LLMs are probabilistic, so the best first use-cases have LOW error cost and EASY verification. Score every candidate on both; the quadrant you want first is high-value + high-feasibility — document summarization with citations, support-triage with human escalation. The trap quadrant is high-value + LOW feasibility — fully automated legal advice, unsupervised medical triage — that's where POCs go to die; either add a human checkpoint and move it right, or defer it. Kill the low-value ones in the meeting, on the record — an architect who says 'no' early builds trust for the 'yes' that matters.

scenes.title: A use-case scorecard you can defend
scenes.body:
USE-CASE SCORECARD (score 1–5 each, justify in one line)

  VALUE
    v1  Measurable baseline exists?        3  "5 hrs/wk manual triage"
    v2  Who feels the pain? (CXO > team)   4  "VP Support owns the KPI"
    v3  Annualized impact ($ or hrs)       4  "~260 hrs/yr → ~$40k"

  FEASIBILITY
    f1  Output verifiable / has citations? 5  "citations checked by agent"
    f2  Error tolerance + human in loop?   4  "human sends final reply"
    f3  Data access + quality ready?       3  "tickets OK, KB needs cleanup"
    f4  Latency/shape fits LLM strengths?  5  "async batch, not realtime"

  Gate: VALUE ≥ 12 AND FEASIBILITY ≥ 16  →  POC candidate
        High value + low feasibility    →  add human checkpoint first
        Anything below                →  kill in the meeting, on record
annot: The one-line justification is the point — scores without reasons are politics
Feasibility weights verification — GA-01's probabilistic nature made concrete
A written kill decision saves three months of zombie POC later

scenes.title: Reference architectures & the build-vs-buy decision
scenes.sub: Every GenAI system is a composition of five blocks — buy or build each one
scenes.narration: Underneath the variety, nearly every GenAI system composes the same five blocks: a MODEL endpoint, a RETRIEVAL layer, an ORCHESTRATION loop, a GUARDRAIL boundary, and an OBSERVABILITY plane — GA-10 through GA-29 taught you each one by hand; a reference architecture is the map of which parts your system needs and how they connect. Then the oldest question in architecture: build vs buy. BUILD when the thing is your differentiator — nobody wins on their embedding store, so buy that; maybe your orchestration IS the product — a coding-agent company builds its loop, a bank configures one. BUY the commodity: model endpoints (GA-29), vector search, content safety. The framework for each block: if it's standard and undifferentiated → buy; if it's standard but needs assembly → configure (open-source + your glue); if it's where you win → build. Write the decision down per block, with the reason — a year from now, someone will ask 'why not just...' and your past self should answer.

Every system you've built this course: same five blocks.
Buy undifferentiated blocks; build the one you win on.
annot: The map makes build-vs-buy a per-block decision — not a religious platform war
Guardrails wrap BOTH sides of the orchestration — AG-09's boundary is architectural
Observability is a plane, not an afterthought — AG-20/21 saw everything the loop did

scenes.title: NFRs for GenAI: latency, accuracy, cost — the triangle that rules everything
scenes.sub: The non-functional requirements checklist nobody hands you
scenes.narration: Classic NFRs — availability, scalability, security — carry over unchanged; GenAI adds three that dominate. ACCURACY as an SLO: define it measurably — task success rate on a golden eval set (AG-21), citation faithfulness, groundedness scores — and set the target per release with evals in CI; 'it feels better' is not an SLO. LATENCY: token-level truth from GA-07 — time-to-first-token and tokens-per-second are user-visible; streaming is the standard mitigation; know your budget per interaction type — a coding agent tolerates 30 seconds, a chat widget dies at 3. COST: token economics from AG-23 — measure cost PER COMPLETED TASK, not per token, and model it: (tokens-in x price + tokens-out x price + retrieval + infra) x volume, with cache hit-rates and prompt-trimming included. These three form a triangle — improve one, budget the other two explicitly. And write NFRs BEFORE the POC: 'accurate enough' defined after the demo is how production incidents happen.

scenes.title: A cost model you can put in a spreadsheet
scenes.body:
MONTHLY COST = TASKS × COST-PER-TASK

COST-PER-TASK =
    (tokens_in  × $in  +  tokens_out × $out)   ← LLM calls/task
  + retrieval_per_task                          ← search + embedding
  + guardrail_per_task                          ← safety screening
  + infra_share                                 ← compute, storage, observability

Worked example (support-triage agent, per task):
  2 LLM calls × (6k in @ $2.50/M + 800 out @ $10/M)
    = 2 × ($0.0150 + $0.0080)   = $0.046
  retrieval + guardrail + infra share          = $0.014
  COST-PER-TASK                                ≈ $0.06
  40k tasks/mo                                 ≈ $2,400/mo
  vs baseline: 260 human-hours × $150         = $39,000/mo

Optimizers: cache (AG-23) → trim context (AG-13)
             → smaller model for easy steps (GA-27)
annot: Cost per COMPLETED task — AG-23's rule; failed retries multiply the LLM line silently
The human-baseline column is what makes the ROI conversation honest
Every optimizer cross-references a reel you already own — the toolkit compounds

scenes.title: POC to production: gates, risk register, client communication
scenes.sub: The last mile is process, not technology — and it's where most GenAI projects die
scenes.narration: A POC proves the technology CAN work; production proves it works RELIABLY, SAFELY, and CHEAPLY — those are different projects, and the bridge is a set of explicit gates. GATE 1 — EVAL: golden-set accuracy meets the SLO across adversarial cases (AG-21), not just the happy path; GATE 2 — SAFETY: red-team results (AG-22), guardrails tested, incident runbook written; GATE 3 — SCALE: load test at 2x expected peak, cost per task within budget, latency within SLO; GATE 4 — OPERATE: dashboards live, alerts tuned, rollback rehearsed, on-call knows what this thing does. Keep a RISK REGISTER — hallucination, prompt injection, data leakage, vendor drift, cost spike — each with likelihood, impact, and a MITIGATION that names a reel you built. Finally, CLIENT COMMUNICATION: demo the failure modes on purpose — showing the eval results and the guardrails earns more trust than a perfect demo, because your audience has already seen a perfect demo fail in production. The architect's product isn't the system — it's the confidence.

scenes.title: Gates and risk register — as living documents
scenes.body:
POC → PRODUCTION GATES
  G1 EVAL      golden-set pass ≥ SLO + adversarial suite   [owner: ML]
  G2 SAFETY    red-team closed, guardrails tested, runbook  [owner: Sec]
  G3 SCALE     2× peak load, cost/task in budget, SLO met   [owner: Eng]
  G4 OPERATE   dashboards, alerts, rollback rehearsed       [owner: SRE]

RISK REGISTER (likelihood × impact → mitigation → reel)
  hallucinated fact      M×H  → citations + eval gating     GA-10/AG-21
  prompt injection       M×H  → input/output screening     AG-09/AG-22
  data leakage via RAG   L×H  → ACL-aware retrieval        GA-10/GA-29
  vendor model drift     M×M  → pinned deployments        GA-29
  cost spike             M×M  → per-task budget alerts    AG-23

Rule: a gate without an owner is a wish.
Rule: a risk without a named mitigation is a hope.
annot: Owner per gate — the difference between a checklist and an audit trail
Each mitigation cites the reel that teaches it — your learning IS the mitigation library
Demo the failures on purpose — confidence is the deliverable, not the demo

recap: Select use-cases on value x feasibility — kill weak ones in the meeting; high-value + low-feasibility needs a human checkpoint first
Every GenAI system composes five blocks — model, retrieval, orchestration, guardrails, observability; buy undifferentiated blocks, build the one you win on
GenAI's NFR triangle: accuracy SLO (evals in CI), latency (TTFT + streaming), cost per completed task — optimize one, budget the other two
POC to production runs through gates — eval, safety, scale, operate — each with an owner; demo failure modes on purpose to earn trust

quiz.q: A use-case scores high on value but low on feasibility (output hard to verify, high error cost). What's the architect's move?
opts: Kill it immediately — low feasibility is a permanent disqualifier
Add a human-in-the-loop checkpoint so error cost drops, then reassess feasibility
Build the POC anyway and let the results decide
Switch to a smaller model to make it feasible
quiz.why: Feasibility is often a function of system design, not the problem. A human checkpoint converts 'unsupervised legal advice' (fatal) into 'lawyer-reviewed drafting' (shippable) — you move the use-case right on the matrix instead of killing value.

quiz.q: Which five blocks make up nearly every GenAI reference architecture?
opts: Model endpoint, retrieval layer, orchestration loop, guardrail boundary, observability plane
Data lake, feature store, training pipeline, serving layer, monitor
quiz.why: That's the pattern map built across the course — GA-03/29 (model), GA-09/10 (retrieval), AG-14/15 (orchestration), AG-09 (guardrails), AG-20/21 (observability). Build-vs-buy is decided block by block.

quiz.q: Why is 'cost per completed task' the right cost metric — not cost per token?
opts: Token prices change too often to budget against
Users experience tasks, not tokens — and failed retries silently multiply token spend, so per-task cost with a human-baseline comparison is the only honest ROI number
Per-token pricing is only available on Azure
Per-task cost is easier to log
quiz.why: A task that takes 4 LLM calls and 2 retries costs very different tokens than one call with no retries. Per-task cost folds in retries, retrieval, guardrails, and infra — and comparing it to the human baseline is what makes the business case real (AG-23's discipline).

code.title: The architect's one-page scorecard
code.body:
USE-CASE      value  feas.  decision   owner
support-triage  11     17     POC ✓      VP Support
contract-draft  14     11     +human HITL Legal
auto-approvals  13      6     KILL       (recorded)

GATES:  G1 eval ✓  G2 safety ✓  G3 scale ✓  G4 operate ✓
NFRs:   accuracy ≥ 92% on golden set (CI-gated)
        TTFT < 800ms, streaming on
        cost/task ≤ $0.08 @ 40k tasks/mo
RISKS:  5 open, 4 mitigated — each cites a reel

One page. Defensible. Signed.
annot: Everything on one page — if the decision needs a deck, it isn't decided
The kill decision recorded next to the wins — that's what makes the next 'yes' credible
NFR targets written BEFORE the POC — 'accurate enough' is defined before the demo, not after the incident

notes:
# Architect Toolkit — GA notes

## Use-case selection
- Axes: **value** (measurable baseline, owner, annualized impact) x **feasibility** (verifiability, error tolerance + human loop, data readiness, latency fit).
- High value + low feasibility → don't kill, add a human checkpoint and re-score.
- Kill low-value on the record — it buys credibility for the real 'yes'.

## Reference architecture
Five blocks: model endpoint · retrieval · orchestration · guardrails · observability.
Build-vs-buy per block: undifferentiated → buy; standard-needs-assembly → configure; differentiating → build. Record reasons.

## NFRs (GenAI-specific)
- **Accuracy**: SLO on a golden eval set (AG-21); evals in CI.
- **Latency**: TTFT + tokens/sec are user-visible (GA-07); streaming is standard; budget per interaction type.
- **Cost**: per completed task = LLM calls + retrieval + guardrails + infra; compare to human baseline.
- Triangle: improve one, budget the other two explicitly.

## POC → production gates
G1 eval · G2 safety · G3 scale · G4 operate — each with an OWNER.
Risk register: likelihood x impact → named mitigation → cites the reel that teaches it.
Client communication: demo the failure modes on purpose. Confidence is the deliverable.
